content: 1. G. Kosatsky, T. Katsouyanni, A. Analitis, et al. conducted a study on the impact of heat on mortality across 15 European cities, published in Epidemiology in 2008. The study highlights the significant relationship between heat exposure and increased mortality rates, emphasizing the need for public health interventions during heatwaves. 2. Yoshino H., Yoshino Y., Zhang Q., et al. explored the indoor thermal environment and energy-saving strategies for urban residential buildings in China. Their findings, published in Energy & Buildings in 2006, provide insights into optimizing indoor thermal comfort while reducing energy consumption. 3. Franck U., Krüger M., Schwarz N., et al. examined heat stress in urban areas by comparing indoor and outdoor temperatures across different urban structures during a heatwave in Leipzig. Their study, published in Meteorologische Zeitschrift in 2013, also assessed subjective well-being under extreme heat conditions. 4. Nguyen J., Schwartz J., Dockery D. investigated the relationship between indoor and outdoor temperature, apparent temperature, relative humidity, and absolute humidity. Their findings, published in Indoor Air in 2014, contribute to understanding how environmental factors influence indoor thermal conditions. 5. Quinn A., Tamerius JD., Perzanowski M., et al. developed a predictive model for indoor heat exposure risk during extreme heat events. Published in Science of the Total Environment in 2014, the study underscores the importance of identifying vulnerable populations and implementing protective measures. 6. Senanayake IP., Welivitiya WDDP., Nadeeka PM. utilized remote sensing to analyze urban heat islands and vegetation cover in Colombo, Sri Lanka, using Landsat-7 ETM+ data. Their study, published in Urban Climate in 2013, highlights the role of vegetation in mitigating urban heat effects. 7. Ashtiani A., Mirzaei PA., Haghighat F. compared artificial neural network and regression methods for predicting indoor thermal conditions in urban heat islands. Their research, published in Energy & Buildings in 2014, provides advanced modeling techniques for urban climate studies. 8. White-Newsome JL., Sánchez BN., Jolliet O., et al. examined the effects of climate change on indoor heat exposure in vulnerable populations. Published in Environmental Research in 2012, the study emphasizes the need for adaptive strategies to protect at-risk groups. 9. Smargiassi A., Fournier M., Griot C., et al. proposed an in-time regression mapping approach to predict indoor temperatures in urban areas. Their study, published in the Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology in 2008, offers a novel method for urban temperature monitoring. 10. Tamerius J., Perzanowski M., Acosta L., et al. analyzed socioeconomic and meteorological determinants of indoor temperature and humidity in New York City dwellings. Published in Weather, Climate, and Society in 2013, the study highlights disparities in indoor environmental conditions. 11. Wang Z., Zhang L., Zhao J., He Y. investigated thermal comfort in naturally ventilated residential buildings in Harbin, China. Their findings, published in Energy & Buildings in 2010, provide guidelines for improving thermal comfort in cold climates. 12. Adunola A. evaluated urban residential thermal comfort in relation to indoor and outdoor air temperatures in Ibadan, Nigeria. Published in Building & Environment in 2014, the study emphasizes the importance of designing thermally comfortable urban housing. 13. Djongyang N., Tchinda R. conducted a field study on thermal comfort and residential thermal environments in intertropical sub-Saharan Africa during the Harmattan season. Their findings, published in Energy Conversion & Management in 2010, provide insights into regional thermal challenges. 14. Indraganti M. studied thermal comfort in naturally ventilated apartments during summer in Hyderabad, India. Published in Applied Energy in 2010, the research highlights the effectiveness of natural ventilation in maintaining thermal comfort. 15. Deng QL., Li NP., Cui YH. measured and analyzed the indoor environment of a high-rise residential building in China's hot summer and cold winter region. Their findings, presented at the 10th International Conference on Indoor Air Quality and Climate in 2005, provide valuable data for improving indoor air quality. 16. Sakka A., Santamouris M., Livada I., et al. assessed the thermal performance of low-income housing during heatwaves. Published in Energy & Buildings in 2012, the study underscores the need for energy-efficient housing solutions for vulnerable populations. 17. Abdul-Wahab SA., Salem N., Ali S. evaluated indoor air quality in a museum and residential homes in Oman. Published in Indoor & Built Environment in 2015, the study highlights the importance of maintaining air quality in diverse indoor settings. 18. Sackou JK., Oga SA., Tanoh F., et al. investigated the relationship between indoor environment and respiratory symptoms among children under five in peri-urban Abidjan. Published in Indoor & Built Environment in 2014, the study emphasizes the health impacts of poor indoor air quality. 19. Dengel A., Swainson M., Ormandy D., Ezratty V. reviewed the issue of overheating in dwellings. Published by the Building Research Establishment in London in 2016, the report provides recommendations for mitigating overheating risks. 20. Gasparrini A., Guo Y., Hashizume M., et al. conducted a multicountry observational study on mortality risks attributable to high and low ambient temperatures. Published in The Lancet in 2015, the study highlights the global health burden of temperature extremes. 21. The World Health Organization published guidelines on natural ventilation for infection control in healthcare settings in 2009. These guidelines emphasize the role of ventilation in reducing the spread of infectious diseases. 22. Bélanger D., Abdous B., Gosselin P., et al. developed an adaptation index to high summer heat associated with adverse health impacts in deprived neighborhoods. Published in Climatic Change in 2015, the study provides a tool for assessing community vulnerability. 23. Peden M. authored the World Report on Child Injury Prevention, published by the World Health Organization in 2008. The report outlines strategies for reducing child injuries globally. 24. Turner S., Arthur G., Lyons RA., et al. reviewed home environment modifications for reducing injuries. Published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2011, the study evaluates the effectiveness of various interventions. 25. The National Safety Council published Injury Facts in 2016, providing comprehensive data on injury trends and prevention strategies. 26. Runyan CW., Casteel C., Perkis D., et al. analyzed unintentional injuries in U.S. homes, focusing on mortality. Published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine in 2005, the study highlights the leading causes of home-related deaths. 27. Moore R. contributed a chapter on housing accidents in the book Housing and Health in Europe: The WHO LARES Project, edited by Ormandy D. and published by Routledge in 2009. The chapter discusses the relationship between housing conditions and health outcomes. 28. The World Health Organization published The Global Burden of Disease: 2004 Update in 2008, providing a comprehensive assessment of global health challenges. 29. The Injury Surveillance Thailand report (2005–2010) provides data on severe injuries and their causes, published in 2012. 30. Wainiqolo I., Kafoa B., Kool B., et al. profiled injury patterns in Fiji using a population-based injury surveillance system. Published in BMC Public Health in 2012, the study identifies key risk factors for injuries. 31. Jangnoor J., Surawera W., Keay L., et al. examined childhood and adult mortality from unintentional falls in India. Published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2011, the study highlights the public health burden of falls. 32. Prüss-Ustün A., Wolf J., Corvalán C., et al. assessed the global burden of disease from environmental risks in the WHO report Preventing Disease Through Healthy Environments, published in 2016. 33. Khambalia A., Joshi P., Brussoni M., et al. conducted a systematic review of risk factors for unintentional injuries due to falls in children aged 0–6 years. Published in Injury Prevention in 2006, the study identifies modifiable risk factors. 34. Carter SE., Campbell EM., Sanson-Fisher RW., et al. investigated environmental hazards in the homes of older people. Published in Age & Ageing in 1997, the study highlights the need for targeted interventions to reduce fall risks.
